title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

State the four necessary and sufficient conditions for deadlock
Detect deadlock using a resource allocation graph
Explain the Banker’s Algorithm and evaluate a state as safe or unsafe
Compare prevention, avoidance, and detection/recovery strategies and identify when each is appropriate

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
section: Four Cars at a Four-Way Stop
text:
Four Cars at a Four-Way Stop
Four cars arrive at a four-way stop simultaneously. Each one needs to cross, and each can only proceed when the opposing traffic clears. But each car is also blocking the opposing traffic for one of the others. Nobody moves. Nobody will ever move. This is deadlock.
In computing: a set of processes where each one is waiting for a resource held by another, and none can ever proceed without external intervention. Deadlock is not a crash — the processes are alive and technically “running,” just permanently suspended waiting for something that will never happen. It’s often harder to detect than a crash for exactly this reason.






Opening Activity: The Dining Philosophers



Five philosophers sit at a round table with a bowl of rice in the middle. Between each pair of neighbors lies one chopstick. To eat, a philosopher needs both adjacent chopsticks. They alternate between thinking (needs nothing) and eating (needs two chopsticks).
Before I explain anything: in small groups, try to design a rule set that lets all five philosophers eat eventually, with no deadlock and no starvation. You have 3 minutes.
We’ll compare solutions after discussing the formal conditions.

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
The Four Necessary Conditions
Deadlock can only arise if all four conditions hold simultaneously. Remove any one and deadlock is impossible.
Mutual exclusion: at least one resource must be held exclusively — only one process can use it at a time. Most I/O devices, write-mode file locks, and mutexes are mutually exclusive by design.
Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting for additional resources held by others. The dangerous pattern: acquire A, then try to acquire B while still holding A.
No preemption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away. A process releases resources only voluntarily when done with them. You can’t just yank a lock out of a process’s hands.
Circular wait: there exists a circular chain {P0, P1, …, Pn} where P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 waits for one held by P2, …, and Pn waits for one held by P0.






Board Exercise: Identify the Conditions



Two processes, two semaphores:
Process P1:      Process P2:
  semWait(s1)      semWait(s2)
  semWait(s2)      semWait(s1)
P1 acquires s1, P2 acquires s2, then each tries for the other’s semaphore.
Identify which of the four conditions is satisfied in this scenario. Which condition would you eliminate to prevent the deadlock, and what would that change about the code?

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Resource Allocation Graphs
A resource allocation graph visualizes deadlock conditions. Processes are circles; resources are rectangles (dots inside represent instances). An arrow from process to resource means “waiting for”; an arrow from resource to process means “allocated to.”
Key rules:

No cycle → no deadlock possible
Cycle, one instance per resource type → deadlock
Cycle, multiple instances per resource type → possible deadlock, needs further analysis

The diagrams below use dashed arrows (→ ·· ·→) for request edges and solid arrows (→) for assignment edges.

Example 1: No Cycle — No Deadlock
P1 holds R1 and is waiting for R2. P2 holds R2 and is not waiting for anything. There is no cycle: following the arrows never brings you back to where you started.





%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#dbeafe', 'primaryBorderColor': '#3b82f6'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    P1((P1)):::process
    P2((P2)):::process
    R1[R1]:::resource
    R2[R2]:::resource

    R1 --> P1
    R2 --> P2
    P1 -.->|requests| R2

    classDef process fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a5f
    classDef resource fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#78350f






P2 can finish and release R2 at any time — P1 is merely waiting, not deadlocked. The system will make progress.


Example 2: Cycle with Single-Instance Resources — Deadlock
P1 holds R1 and requests R2. P2 holds R2 and requests R1. Each is waiting for the other to release something neither will ever release.





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart LR
    P1((P1)):::process
    P2((P2)):::process
    R1[R1]:::resource
    R2[R2]:::resource

    R1 -->|assigned| P1
    R2 -->|assigned| P2
    P1 -.->|requests| R2
    P2 -.->|requests| R1

    classDef process fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d
    classDef resource fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#78350f






Trace the cycle: P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1. Every node in the cycle is permanently blocked. This is the deadlock from the semaphore example earlier in the lecture with s1/s2.


Example 3: Cycle with Multi-Instance Resources — Not Necessarily Deadlock
R1 has two instances. P1 holds one instance of R1 and requests R2. P2 holds R2 and requests R1. P3 holds the other instance of R1 and needs nothing else.





%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart LR
    P1((P1)):::process
    P2((P2)):::process
    P3((P3)):::process
    R1["R1\n● ●"]:::resource
    R2[R2]:::resource

    R1 -->|inst 1| P1
    R1 -->|inst 2| P3
    R2 -->|assigned| P2
    P1 -.->|requests| R2
    P2 -.->|requests| R1

    classDef process fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#14532d
    classDef resource fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#78350f






There is a cycle (P1 → R2 → P2 → R1 → P1), but it is not a deadlock. P3 holds R1 instance 2 and isn’t waiting for anything — P3 can finish and release its instance. That frees R1 for P2, which can then finish and release R2, which unblocks P1. The safe sequence is P3 → P2 → P1.
The key lesson: a cycle is a necessary condition for deadlock with single-instance resources, but not sufficient when resources have multiple instances.


Example 4: Three Processes — Deadlock Detection Exercise
This is the graph you should be able to draw and analyze from scratch:

P1 holds R2, requests R1
P2 holds nothing, requests R1 and R2 (it has requested both but neither is granted yet — R1 has one instance, R2 has one instance, both are held)
P3 holds R1, requests R2






%%{init: {'theme': 'base'}}%%
flowchart LR
    P1((P1)):::process
    P2((P2)):::process
    P3((P3)):::process
    R1[R1]:::resource
    R2[R2]:::resource

    R2 -->|assigned| P1
    R1 -->|assigned| P3
    P1 -.->|requests| R1
    P2 -.->|requests| R1
    P2 -.->|requests| R2
    P3 -.->|requests| R2

    classDef process fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#7f1d1d
    classDef resource fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#78350f






Two cycles exist here: P1 → R1 → P3 → R2 → P1, and P2 → R1 → P3 → R2 → P2. Since both resources have only one instance, both cycles confirm deadlock. P1, P2, and P3 are all permanently blocked.






Board Exercise: Draw the Graph



Draw the resource allocation graph for the semaphore example above (P1 holds s1/requests s2, P2 holds s2/requests s1). Does it contain a cycle? Now add a third semaphore s3 and a third process P3 that holds s3 and waits for s1. Add P1 also wanting s3. Is the system now definitely deadlocked, or only possibly?

title: 07 · Deadlock & Starvation
text:
Strategies for Handling Deadlock
Three fundamentally different approaches, each suitable for different situations.

Prevention: Make One Condition Impossible
Design the system so at least one necessary condition can never hold. This is conservative but guarantees no deadlock.
Attacking mutual exclusion — generally impossible for devices and write locks. Some resources (read-only data, immutable files) are inherently shareable, but most aren’t.
Attacking hold-and-wait — require processes to request all resources upfront before execution begins. If they can’t get everything immediately, they get nothing and wait. Eliminates hold-and-wait but is deeply impractical: most programs can’t enumerate all their resource needs before running, and early-acquiring resources wastes them.
Attacking no preemption — allow the OS to forcibly reclaim resources. If P1 holds A and requests B but B is unavailable, take A away; P1 restarts from scratch. Works for CPU registers and memory pages; doesn’t work for half-written files or in-progress I/O.
Attacking circular wait — impose a global ordering on resource types and require every process to request in that order. If all processes must request R1 before R2 before R3, no circular chain can form. This is practical and widely used: Linux kernel developers follow strict documented lock-ordering conventions specifically to prevent deadlock in kernel code.


Avoidance: Never Enter an Unsafe State
Allow the four conditions but refuse resource requests that might lead to deadlock. Requires knowing processes’ maximum resource needs upfront.
A state is safe if there exists at least one sequence in which all processes can finish. The OS checks before each allocation: does a safe ordering still exist after this grant? If yes, grant it. If no, deny and make the process wait.
The Banker’s Algorithm is the classical avoidance approach, named for how a bank manages loan risk. It uses four data structures:

Available[j] — how many instances of resource Rj are currently free
Max[i][j] — the maximum instances of Rj that process Pi might ever request
Allocation[i][j] — instances of Rj currently held by Pi
Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j] — remaining potential requests from Pi

(Answer: P1 can run first with (3,3,2). After P1 releases, Available becomes (5,3,2). Then P3, P4, P0, P2 — safe sequence exists.)


The Banker’s Algorithm’s limitation: it requires knowing maximum resource needs in advance, assumes a fixed set of processes and resources, and is impractical for most real applications. It’s elegant as a design principle; real OSes rarely implement it directly.


Detection and Recovery: Let It Happen, Then Break It
Allow deadlock to occur. Periodically check for it. When found, break it. This is common for resources that can’t easily be made preemptible or for systems where deadlock is rare.
Detection requires cycle detection in the resource allocation graph (for single-instance resources) or a matrix algorithm similar to the Banker’s (for multiple instances). Check frequency is a design decision: more frequent checks find deadlocks faster but consume CPU.
Process termination recovery: kill one or more deadlocked processes to break the cycle. Choose which to kill based on priority, runtime so far, resources held, and impact on other processes. Aborting all deadlocked processes is simple but brutal; aborting one at a time is surgical but requires re-running detection after each.
Resource preemption recovery: forcibly take a resource from one process and give it to another. The victim process rolls back to a checkpoint. Risk: the same process may be repeatedly victimized (starvation at the recovery level). Fix: include rollback count in the victim-selection cost function.






Discussion Prompt



Return to the dining philosophers solutions your groups proposed at the start. Classify each solution: does it use prevention (which condition?), avoidance, or detection/recovery? Does it guarantee no starvation as well as no deadlock? Which solution would you actually implement in production code, and why?

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain what the three layers of scheduling (long-term, medium-term, short-term) each control
Calculate average wait time and turnaround time for FCFS, SJF, SRTF, and Round Robin
Explain the convoy effect, Belady’s Anomaly, and starvation, and which algorithms suffer from each
Describe why preemption is necessary for interactive systems and what race conditions it can introduce

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
The Problem Scheduling Solves
Imagine a single CPU and a dozen processes all wanting to run. Some are playing music — needs the CPU regularly, in short bursts, with tight timing. Some are compiling code — needs the CPU for long stretches. Some are waiting on network responses — mostly idle, short bursts of activity. If the CPU simply ran them in order of arrival, a long compilation would block music playback entirely. The user experience would be terrible.
Scheduling is the OS’s answer to: which process gets the CPU next, and for how long? The algorithm it chooses determines how responsive the system feels, how efficiently the CPU is used, and whether any process ever gets permanently starved. There’s no perfect algorithm — every design involves tradeoffs — which is why modern OSes use different schedulers for different situations.

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Three Layers of Scheduling
Long-term scheduling decides which programs get admitted into the system as processes. It controls the degree of multiprogramming — how many processes exist at once. More processes means smaller slices of CPU and memory per process, but potentially higher throughput. In most desktop OSes this is implicit (every launched app just runs), but in batch and production systems it’s explicit and important.
Medium-term scheduling handles swapping — moving processes between memory and disk based on memory pressure. When memory is scarce, it suspends processes to free space; when pressure eases, it revives them. This directly controls how many processes actively compete for the CPU.
Short-term scheduling — the dispatcher — is what people usually mean by “the scheduler.” It runs extremely frequently, potentially thousands of times per second, and makes the fine-grained decision of which ready process runs next. It fires on clock interrupts, I/O completions, new arrivals to the ready queue, and whenever the current process blocks.

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
What Makes a Good Scheduler?
Goals differ based on who you’re optimizing for.
From the user’s perspective: turnaround time (submission to completion, relevant for batch) and response time (action to visible reaction, critical for interactive). Predictability matters too — a scheduler that’s usually 2 seconds but occasionally 30 creates a poor experience even if the average is acceptable.
From the system’s perspective: throughput (jobs completed per unit time) and processor utilization (keep the CPU busy, especially on expensive shared hardware). Fairness and priority enforcement also matter: high-priority processes should run first, and no process should be starved indefinitely.
These goals conflict. Maximizing response time for interactive processes may require preempting a long-running batch job that was making excellent throughput progress. There is no universally best scheduling algorithm — only algorithms better suited to different workloads.

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Preemptive vs. Nonpreemptive Scheduling
Nonpreemptive schedulers let the running process keep the CPU until it voluntarily gives it up — by blocking on I/O, yielding, or terminating. Once selected, it runs until it stops.
Preemptive schedulers can forcibly remove the CPU from a running process — via a timer interrupt — and give it to another. Essential for interactive systems requiring predictable response times. All modern OSes (Linux, Windows, macOS) are preemptive.
The tradeoff: preemption requires a context switch with its associated overhead. Without preemption, a CPU-bound process can monopolize the CPU and starve everything else.
Preemption also introduces race conditions: Process A is halfway through updating shared data when it’s preempted. Process B runs and reads the half-modified structure. The data is inconsistent. This is exactly why shared data in concurrent programs requires synchronization — Lecture 6.

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Scheduling Algorithms

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
Processes run in the order they arrive. Nonpreemptive. Simple to implement.
Suffers from the convoy effect: short processes stuck behind a long one inherit all of its wait time.






Board Exercise: FCFS



Three processes arrive simultaneously: P1 (burst 24ms), P2 (burst 3ms), P3 (burst 3ms).
Draw the Gantt chart, then calculate:

Average wait time: (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17ms

Now reverse the order — P2, P3, P1 — and recalculate:

Average wait time: (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = 3ms

Same work, same CPU time — but the order changes average wait from 17ms to 3ms. This is the motivation for SJF.




Shortest Job First (SJF)
Run the process with the shortest expected CPU burst next. Nonpreemptive.
SJF is provably optimal for minimizing average waiting time in nonpreemptive settings. The catch: you need to know burst lengths in advance, which typically requires estimation from historical averages.


Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
The preemptive version of SJF: when a new process arrives, if its burst is shorter than the remaining time of the current process, preempt. Optimal for minimizing average wait time in the preemptive setting. Risk: starvation of long processes if short ones keep arriving.






Board Exercise: SJF vs. SRTF



Four processes:



Process
Arrival
Burst




P1
0
8


P2
1
4


P3
2
9


P4

5



Draw the Gantt chart for nonpreemptive SJF, then for SRTF (preemptive SJF). Compare average wait times. SRTF should give a lower average — why doesn’t it always win in practice?




Round Robin (RR)
Preemptive. Each process gets a fixed time quantum q (typically 10–100ms). After q elapses, the process is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue.
With n processes and quantum q, every process gets CPU time within (n−1)q — a hard bound on wait time that FCFS and SJF don’t offer.
The choice of q dominates performance:

Large q → approaches FCFS (processes rarely preempted)
Small q → maximum responsiveness, but if q < context switch time, you spend more time switching than executing







Board Exercise: Round Robin



Three processes: P1 (burst 24ms), P2 (burst 3ms), P3 (3ms). Quantum = 4ms.
Draw the Gantt chart. Calculate average wait time and compare to FCFS from the first exercise. Which is better for the short processes? Which for the long process? (Takeaway: RR distributes wait time more fairly but may hurt overall throughput.)




Priority Scheduling
Associate a numeric priority with each process; always run the highest priority. Can be preemptive or nonpreemptive. When priorities tie, SJF or SRTF applies.
Starvation risk: low-priority processes may never run if high-priority ones keep arriving. Aging fixes this: gradually increase a process’s priority the longer it waits. Eventually, even the lowest-priority job gets scheduled.
Real-world priority tiers:



Priority
Process Type




Highest
Real-time (hard deadlines)


High
System/kernel


Medium
Interactive user


Low
Batch background



Each tier can have its own queue with its own algorithm — Round Robin for interactive, FCFS for batch.

title: 05 · Uniprocessor Scheduling
text:
Dispatcher Latency
The dispatcher performs the actual context switch once the scheduler has chosen the next process. Dispatcher latency is the time between the selection and the process actually starting execution — it includes saving the outgoing state, loading the incoming state, and the cache cold-start penalty. Minimizing dispatcher latency is a kernel implementation concern, separate from the scheduling algorithm itself.






Discussion Prompt



SJF gives the best average waiting time, so why don’t all OSes use it? Think through: what does the OS actually know at scheduling time? What would happen to long jobs on a busy server that runs SJF? What does “optimal” mean here, and for whom?

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
section: Why counter++ Is Not One Operation
text:
Why counter++ Is Not One Operation
counter++ looks like a single step. At the machine level, it isn’t:

Load the current value from memory into a register
Add 1 to the register
Store the result back to memory

If two threads execute these steps concurrently and their steps interleave, one increment can silently overwrite the other:






Board Exercise: Trace the Race



Thread 1 and Thread 2 both try to increment counter from 42. Trace through this interleaving:
Thread 1: LOAD  counter → register1 = 42
Thread 2: LOAD  counter → register2 = 42   (reads before T1 stores!)
Thread 1: ADD   register1 = 43
Thread 2: ADD   register2 = 43
Thread 1: STORE counter = 43
Thread 2: STORE counter = 43               (overwrites T1's result!)
Result: counter = 43, not 44. One increment was lost.
Now trace an interleaving that produces the correct result. Now trace one that produces the maximum possible loss. (This last one reveals that with 1,000,000 iterations each, the minimum possible result is 1,000,000 — why?)


Race conditions are timing-dependent. They may not appear in testing (if threads don’t interleave badly), may appear rarely in production, and may disappear when you add print statements that change timing. This makes them among the hardest bugs to diagnose.

title: 06 · Concurrency & Mutual Exclusion
text:
Critical Sections
The counter++ code is a critical section: code that accesses shared data and must not execute concurrently. The problem isn’t sharing — sharing is useful. The problem is that some operations on shared data require exclusive access to be correct.
The general structure:
while (true) {
    [entry section]      // request permission to enter
    critical section     // exclusive access to shared data
    [exit section]       // signal that you're done
    remainder section    // can run concurrently
}
Any correct solution must satisfy three requirements:

Mutual exclusion — if Pi is in its CS, no other process is in its CS simultaneously
Progress — if no process is in its CS and some want to enter, a decision is made in finite time; it cannot be postponed indefinitely
Bounded waiting — a process waiting to enter its CS will eventually get in; there’s an upper bound on how many times others can enter first

All three matter. A solution achieving only mutual exclusion might deadlock (violates progress). A solution achieving mutual exclusion and progress might starve one process indefinitely (violates bounded waiting).

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Distinguish loosely coupled, functionally specialized, and tightly coupled (SMP) multiprocessor systems
Explain the tradeoffs between dynamic and static process-to-processor assignment
Compare primary/secondary and peer architectures and identify the failure modes of each
Describe the four thread-scheduling strategies (load sharing, gang, dedicated, dynamic) and the workloads each is suited for

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
section: Why Don’t 8 Cores Give You 8× Speedup?
text:
Why Don’t 8 Cores Give You 8× Speedup?
Buy a laptop with an 8-core processor and run a parallelized program. You probably won’t get 8× faster execution. You might get 4×. Sometimes less. Why?
Not all code can run in parallel. Cores share resources — memory buses, caches — that become bottlenecks under heavy load. Threads need to synchronize and wait for each other. And the OS itself, managing all of this, introduces overhead. Multiprocessor scheduling is the OS’s attempt to assign work to multiple processors as intelligently as possible — and understanding the constraints that make it genuinely hard.






Opening Discussion



Before diving in: can you name a task from everyday computing where you’d expect good parallelism? A task where you’d expect poor parallelism? What’s the difference between them? (Lead toward: embarrassingly parallel work vs. inherently sequential work.)

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Types of Multiprocessor Systems
Not all multiprocessor systems are the same, and the right scheduling strategy depends on the system type.
Loosely coupled (distributed) systems are independent machines with their own memory and I/O, connected by a network. Each machine runs its own OS. Coordination happens through message passing at the application level. Cloud computing clusters are the modern example.
Functionally specialized systems have a primary general-purpose processor that offloads work to specialized processors — a GPU for graphics, a DSP for audio, a network processor for packet handling. Your phone does this. The primary controls the others and feeds them work.
Tightly coupled (SMP) systems have multiple processors sharing physical memory and running under a single OS. This is what “multicore” means in practice — your laptop’s cores share RAM and are coordinated by one kernel. SMP is dominant for everything from laptops to large servers and is the focus of this lecture.

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Synchronization Granularity
Before you can schedule parallel work effectively, you need to understand how often the parallel threads communicate and synchronize. This is granularity:








Grain Size
Description
Sync Interval




Fine
Parallelism within a single instruction stream
< 20 instructions


Medium
Parallel tasks within one application
20–200 instructions


Coarse
Concurrent processes in a multiprogrammed environment
200–2,000 instructions


Very Coarse
Distributed processes across network nodes
2,000–1M instructions


Independent
Unrelated processes, no coordination
N/A



Granularity matters because synchronization has overhead — locking, waiting, signaling, cache invalidation. Fine-grained parallelism (vectorized math, pipeline execution) is usually managed by hardware and compilers, not the OS. Medium-grained parallelism — parallel threads within an application — is where OS scheduling decisions make the biggest difference.

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Assigning Processes to Processors
In an SMP system, the OS decides which core each process runs on. Two approaches:
Dynamic assignment treats all cores as a shared pool. Any process can run on any available core. A single global ready queue services all processors. This achieves excellent load balance and is the dominant approach in modern OSes including Linux and Windows.
Static assignment binds a process to a specific core at creation. That core’s scheduler manages it exclusively until termination. The advantage is reduced scheduling overhead and potentially better cache reuse — the process always runs on the same core, keeping its data warm. The disadvantage is load imbalance: one core can be swamped while another idles.

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Architecture: Who Decides?
Two patterns govern how scheduling decisions are made across processors:
Primary/Secondary architecture: one processor handles all scheduling for the others. The secondaries request work from the primary. Simple to implement — scheduling logic lives in one place, conflicts are easy to resolve. But the primary is both a performance bottleneck (all scheduling traffic flows through one processor) and a single point of failure (if the primary crashes, the system stops).
Peer architecture: every processor runs the kernel and makes its own scheduling decisions from a shared process pool. Better scalability, no single point of failure. Significantly more complex: the OS must ensure two processors don’t pick the same process simultaneously, requiring mutual exclusion on the global ready queue — which itself becomes a contention point under heavy load. Most real SMP OSes use a peer architecture.






Board Exercise: Primary/Secondary Failure



Walk through what happens in a primary/secondary system when: (a) a secondary processor fails, (b) the primary processor fails. Compare to the same scenarios in a peer architecture. Which architecture would you choose for a hospital’s life-support monitoring system, and why?

title: 04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling
text:
Thread Scheduling Strategies
Processes aren’t always the unit of work on multiprocessors — often threads are. Four strategies:
Load sharing extends uniprocessor scheduling to multiple cores. A global queue of threads exists; any idle core pulls from it. Load stays balanced, no central scheduler is needed. The costs: the global queue requires mutual exclusion (contention under heavy load); preempted threads often resume on different cores (cold cache); threads from the same application rarely all run simultaneously (hurting parallelism for tightly-coupled apps).
Gang scheduling assigns a set of related threads to run simultaneously on matching cores — one thread per core, all at once. When the time slice expires, the whole gang is preempted together. This dramatically reduces synchronization overhead: if all threads in a parallel task run at the same time, they can coordinate without waiting on each other to be scheduled. Particularly valuable for scientific simulations, game engines, and parallel database queries.
Gang scheduling can be uniform (all gangs get equal time slices) or weighted (higher-priority gangs get larger slices).
Dedicated processor assignment gives each thread its own processor for the application’s entire lifetime. If a thread blocks, its processor idles. The defense: in high-performance computing with hundreds of cores, processor utilization is no longer the most important metric. If letting a processor idle during a 10ms lock wait allows the overall job to finish 5× faster by eliminating scheduling overhead, the idle time is worth it.
Dynamic scheduling lets the application vary its thread count during execution. The OS responds dynamically: when processors are idle, allocate them to requesting jobs; when a new job arrives and all processors are busy, take one processor from any job currently holding more than one; if no job has more than one processor, the new job waits. This requires cooperation between the OS and application runtime, but achieves good utilization across mixed workloads.






Discussion Prompt



A scientific simulation uses 32 threads that synchronize at a barrier every 15 instructions. A web server handles 500 independent HTTP requests per second. Which scheduling strategy would you recommend for each, and why? What would happen if you applied the wrong strategy?

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Classify security violations using the CIA triad and the five violation categories
Distinguish masqueraders, misfeasors, and clandestine users and explain which mechanisms defend against each
Describe how each layer of the four-layer security model works and what it protects against
Explain the principle of least privilege and apply it to a system design scenario
Compare symmetric and asymmetric cryptography and explain why both are used in practice

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Think Like an Attacker
Security courses usually focus on defenses. This one starts differently: before you can design a defense, you need to understand what you’re defending against.
What does an attacker want? One of a few things:

Access to data they’re not supposed to see (read your files, intercept your traffic, steal credentials)
Ability to modify data they shouldn’t touch (change a grade, alter a transaction, inject malicious code)
Control of a system they don’t own (run code, host malware, mine cryptocurrency on your hardware)
Ability to prevent legitimate use (crash the service, hold files ransom)

Every security mechanism in the OS exists to make one of these goals harder. The uncomfortable truth is that no system is perfectly secure. The goal is to make attacks more expensive than they’re worth, detect breaches when they happen, and limit damage when they succeed anyway.






Opening Discussion



Before diving in: what security violations have you personally experienced or heard about recently? For each one, try to classify it: was it a confidentiality breach, an integrity breach, a denial of service? Who was the attacker — an outsider, an insider, automated malware? (This grounds the abstract framework in things students have actually seen.)

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Security Violation Categories
Security violations map to what the attacker achieves:

Breach of confidentiality — unauthorized access to sensitive data
Breach of integrity — unauthorized modification of data
Breach of availability — unauthorized destruction of data or prevention of access
Theft of service — unauthorized use of system resources
Denial of service (DoS) — preventing legitimate use by flooding or crashing the system

The CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) is the standard framework for thinking about what a security policy must protect. A good system design asks: for each piece of data or resource, who should be able to read it? Who should be able to modify it? How reliably must it be accessible?

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Who’s Attacking?
Two broad sources of threats: humans (intruders) and automated programs (malware). Real attacks often combine both.
Masqueraders are outsiders who steal credentials and impersonate legitimate users. A hacker using a stolen password is a masquerader. Defense: strong authentication — make impersonation hard.
Misfeasors are legitimate insiders who exceed their authorized access — an employee reading HR files they have no business seeing, or an admin abusing privileges for personal gain. Their activity looks legitimate on the surface, making detection hard. Defense: granular access control and auditing.
Clandestine users gain privileged (root/admin) control and use it to disable logging and evade auditing. They attack the accountability layer — the goal is to act without evidence. Defense: tamper-evident logging, privileged operation monitoring.
Each type requires different defenses. The mistake is assuming all attackers look the same.






Class Activity: Classify the Attack



For each scenario, identify the intruder type and the appropriate countermeasure:

A former employee still has VPN credentials three months after leaving the company
A system administrator copies the customer database to a personal laptop
An attacker gains root access and deletes all system logs before exfiltrating data
An employee changes their own salary record in the HR system

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Malware: Structure and Types
Malicious software (malware) falls into two structural categories:
Parasitic malware cannot exist independently — it attaches to legitimate programs and runs when they do. Viruses copy themselves into executables. Logic bombs are dormant code planted in legitimate programs, activating when a condition is met (a specific date, the absence of a particular account, a key input). Backdoors are hidden authentication bypasses — a hardcoded password or extra admin account — that persist after the initial compromise.
Independent malware runs as a standalone process. Worms spread across networks autonomously, exploiting vulnerabilities to replicate from machine to machine without any human action (no need to click an attachment). Bots are compromised machines participating in a botnet — a network of thousands of infected computers used collectively for spam, DDoS attacks, and further attacks.
Notable types:

Trojan horse — looks legitimate, secretly performs malicious actions. Up to 80% of spam has historically been delivered through spyware-infected machines whose owners had no idea.
Ransomware — encrypts your files, demands payment for the key. Key insight: paying doesn’t guarantee recovery. The only reliable defense is offline backups.
Spyware — harvests personal data (browsing habits, passwords, financial info), often bundled with “free” software.

All of these try to exploit or escalate privileges. A compromised web server account might pivot to root via a kernel vulnerability; a phishing email might capture credentials for a low-privilege account that has access to everything.

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
The Principle of Least Privilege
Every user, process, and component should have the minimum access necessary to do its job — no more. Jerome Saltzer articulated this in 1974 for the Multics OS:

“The purpose of this principle is to reduce the number of potential interactions among privileged programs to the minimum necessary to operate correctly, so that one may develop confidence that unintentional, unwanted, or improper uses of privilege do not occur.”

In practice: your web browser shouldn’t have access to your SSH keys. Your text editor shouldn’t make network connections. A compromised application should be limited in what it can destroy. When a breach occurs — and eventually it will — least privilege limits the blast radius.






Board Exercise: Apply Least Privilege



A web application needs to: serve static HTML files, write to a log file, read from a database, and send email notifications.
Design the minimum permission set for the web server process. What should it not be able to do, even though the server runs as a software process on the machine? For each permission you’d deny, explain what attack it prevents.

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Four Layers of Defense
Security is layered — no single mechanism is sufficient, and defeating one layer should still leave others:
Physical security is the foundation. Physical access to a machine bypasses almost all software security. Countermeasures: locked server rooms, security cameras, full-disk encryption (a stolen drive contains only ciphertext), hardware security modules. Physical security is often the weakest link in small organizations.
Network security controls what enters and leaves. Attacks at this layer include packet sniffing (intercepting cleartext traffic), spoofing (forging source addresses), and on-path attacks (impersonating both parties in a communication). Countermeasures: encryption (TLS/HTTPS makes sniffed traffic useless), authentication (cryptographic proof of identity), and filtering (firewalls with strict ingress/egress rules).
Operating system security is where this course has spent most of its time. Attacks target insecure defaults, unpatched vulnerabilities, and misconfigured permissions. Countermeasures include regular patching, hardening (disabling unused services, strict permissions, removing unnecessary SUID binaries), and OS-level sandboxing via namespaces, seccomp filters, and containers.
Application security addresses bugs in software itself: logic errors, improper input validation, and memory safety violations. The buffer overflow attacks in the next lecture are application-layer attacks. Countermeasures include sandboxing applications (limiting which system calls they can make), software signing, and — critically — writing memory-safe code.






Key Pattern: Defense in Depth



An attacker who compromises your web server process should still face network controls preventing lateral movement. An attacker who gets on your network should still face host-based defenses. An attacker who compromises a low-privilege account should face access controls that prevent escalation. No single layer is impenetrable; the goal is that bypassing all of them requires disproportionate effort.

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Authentication and Access Control
Authentication answers: who are you? Access control answers: what are you allowed to do? Both are necessary; neither alone is sufficient.
Authentication factors:



Factor
Type
Example




Something you know
Secret
Password, PIN


Something you have
Token
TOTP authenticator, smart card


Something you are
Biometric
Fingerprint, facial recognition


Something you do
Behavioral
Typing rhythm, mouse dynamics


Somewhere you are
Location
IP geolocation, GPS



Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two or more categories. A stolen password plus no physical token cannot authenticate. MFA is the single most effective defense against credential attacks — which represent the majority of real-world breaches.
An access control system mediates between authenticated users and system resources. It consults an authorization database and either permits or denies each request. An auditing component logs accesses for review and forensics. Access control policies range from discretionary (Unix file permissions — resource owners control access) to mandatory (OS enforces a central policy, no user override) to role-based (users are assigned roles; roles have permissions — used in enterprise systems).

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Intrusion Detection
Prevention is imperfect; detection is essential. An IDS monitors system events and alerts on signs of unauthorized access.
An IDS has three components: sensors collect raw data (network traffic, system call traces, log files); analyzers examine sensor data to determine if an intrusion has occurred; a user interface presents findings and enables response.
Host-based IDS (HIDS) monitors a single machine — file access, system calls, process behavior. Detects attacks invisible to network monitoring. Limited to one host.
Network-based IDS (NIDS) monitors traffic for an entire network segment. Detects scanning, exploit attempts, and exfiltration across many machines simultaneously. Cannot see encrypted traffic or purely local attacks.

title: 09 · OS Security
text:
Cryptography as a Security Tool
Cryptography secures data in transit and at rest by making it unreadable without the right key.
Symmetric cryptography uses the same key for encryption and decryption. Fast; well-suited for bulk data. Challenge: distributing the shared secret securely — you need a secure channel to establish the secret key, which is the very problem you’re trying to solve.
Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a key pair: a public key shared openly and a private key kept secret. Anything encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key. This solves key distribution — publish your public key, and anyone can send you an encrypted message only you can read.
Asymmetric cryptography is computationally expensive; in practice, it’s used only to securely exchange a symmetric session key (as in TLS), which then encrypts actual data traffic.






Discussion Prompt



You’re browsing your bank’s website over HTTPS. An attacker is monitoring your network traffic (on-path).
Walk through what they can and cannot do: - Can they read the contents of your requests? Why or why not? - Can they modify your requests before they reach the bank? - Can they see which server you’re connecting to? - What would need to fail for them to be able to read your traffic?
(This is a good way to ground TLS in a concrete threat model rather than abstract cryptographic promises.)

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain the difference between a process and a thread and what each one owns
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of User-Level Threads vs. Kernel-Level Threads
Describe the three thread states and the four operations that change them
Write and reason about basic pthreads code
Explain why race conditions occur and what fork-join parallelism looks like

title: 03 · Threads
section: Why Can You Scroll While the Page Is Loading?
text:
Why Can You Scroll While the Page Is Loading?
Open a browser and navigate to a heavy website. While images and scripts are still downloading, you can scroll, click, type in the address bar, and switch tabs. How?
The browser isn’t taking turns between downloading and responding to you — it’s doing multiple things genuinely at once, within the same program. One part handles network I/O, another renders what’s already arrived, another listens for your input. These are threads: independent flows of execution sharing the same process.
That’s the thread model in a sentence: shared memory, independent execution. Understanding it changes how you think about performance, about writing concurrent programs, and about why some bugs are so hard to reproduce.

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Processes vs. Threads
Recall from last lecture that a process has two responsibilities: owning resources and executing instructions. Threads split these apart.
A process is the unit of resource ownership. It has a virtual address space, open files, I/O channels, and all the OS bookkeeping that goes with them.
A thread is the unit of execution within a process. It has its own program counter, register set, and stack — the minimum needed to independently track where it is in execution. But it shares the process’s code, data, and file handles with every other thread in the same process.






Board Exercise: What’s Shared, What’s Private?



Draw a process containing three threads. Label which resources are shared across all three threads and which are private to each thread.
Shared: code, data, heap, open files
Private to each thread: program counter, registers, stack
Follow-up: if Thread 1 writes to a global variable, which threads see the change immediately?


This distinction has practical consequences. Creating a new thread is much cheaper than a new process — no new address space, no new file descriptor table, no full PCB copy. Switching between threads in the same process is cheaper — the memory mappings don’t change, so the cache stays warm. And threads can communicate simply by reading and writing shared memory, without pipes, sockets, or any IPC overhead.
The cost is coordination. Because threads share memory, any thread can corrupt any shared data. Without careful synchronization — the subject of Lecture 6 — this produces silent, timing-dependent bugs. Threads make some things simple and other things genuinely hard.

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Thread States and Operations
Thread state mirrors process state, simplified to three values: Running, Ready, and Blocked. The key difference from processes: a blocked thread does not block the other threads in its process. If the download thread blocks on a slow network connection, the render thread and input thread continue running. This is precisely what makes browsers responsive.
Four operations drive state changes: Spawn creates a new thread, Block suspends a thread waiting for an event, Unblock moves a blocked thread back to Ready, and Finish terminates the thread.
Two exceptions: suspending a process suspends all its threads — there’s no way to keep some threads running while the process is swapped out. Terminating a process terminates all threads within it. The process is the container; removing the container removes everything inside.

title: 03 · Threads
text:
User-Level vs. Kernel-Level Threads
The OS doesn’t have to know threads exist. Thread management can happen entirely in user space, invisible to the kernel. Alternatively, the kernel can manage threads directly. Both approaches exist and both have real tradeoffs.
User-Level Threads (ULTs) are managed by a user-space library. The kernel sees only a single-threaded process. Thread operations — creation, switching, scheduling — happen without kernel involvement, making them fast and portable across different OSes.
The problem: when a ULT makes a blocking system call (like reading a file), the kernel blocks the entire process, not just that one thread. All other ULTs freeze. The kernel doesn’t know they exist. This cripples I/O concurrency. The workaround is jacketing — converting blocking calls to non-blocking ones and polling — which is complex and unpleasant to do correctly.
The second problem: on a multiprocessor, only one ULT runs at a time. The kernel allocates exactly one CPU to the process. True parallelism is impossible.
Kernel-Level Threads (KLTs) are managed by the kernel. Each thread is a real scheduling entity. One thread blocking on I/O doesn’t affect the others. Multiple threads can run simultaneously on multiple cores. Windows uses this model.
The cost: every thread operation — creation, context switch, blocking — requires a system call and a mode switch into kernel mode. With many frequently-switching threads, this overhead accumulates.
The combined approach does creation and scheduling in user space (fast) but uses the kernel for CPU assignment (parallel). This is essentially how modern runtimes work — Go’s goroutines, Java virtual threads, Python’s asyncio — many lightweight user-space units multiplexed onto a smaller pool of kernel threads.






Discussion Prompt



Chrome uses a multi-process architecture — each tab runs in its own process, not just its own thread. What reliability benefit does this give? What’s the performance cost compared to a purely multi-threaded design? Is the tradeoff worth it?

title: 03 · Threads
03 · Threads
text:
Multicore Programming
Having multiple cores available doesn’t make programs faster automatically. Concurrent execution means tasks make progress interleaved over time — possible even on a single core through rapid switching. Parallel execution means tasks run at literally the same instant on different cores — requires multiple cores. Parallelism implies concurrency; concurrency does not imply parallelism.
Using threads well on multicore hardware requires thinking carefully about: how to divide work, how to balance load across cores, how threads share data, which computations depend on others’ results, and how to test and debug behavior that varies with timing.

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Fork-Join Parallelism
Fork-join is the cleanest pattern for expressing parallel work: break a problem into subproblems, fork a thread for each, and join when all are done.
if problem is small enough:
    solve the problem directly

else: (problem is large or can be broken down)
    subtask1 = fork(new Task(subset of problem))
    subtask2 = fork(new Task(subset of problem))

    result1 = join(subtask1)
    result2 = join(subtask2)

    return result1 combined with result2
Merge sort, parallel reduce, map-reduce — all are fork-join at heart. Fork creates parallel execution; join synchronizes results. Java’s ForkJoinPool, Go’s goroutines with channels, and Rust’s Rayon library all implement variations of this.

title: 03 · Threads
text:
Threading Gotchas
When fork() is called from a multithreaded process, Linux creates a child with only a single thread — the one that called fork(). The other parent threads don’t exist in the child. This is a subtle trap: if the parent’s threads held any locks at the moment of the fork, the child process inherits those locks in a locked state that can never be unlocked. Programs that mix fork() and threads must handle this carefully.
exec() in a multithreaded context replaces the entire process — all threads — with the new program, which starts fresh with a single thread. No surprises there.






Discussion Prompt



A ULT makes a blocking read from the network. All other ULTs in that process freeze. Describe two approaches to avoid this without switching to KLTs. What are the downsides of each? This is a real engineering problem that Node.js, Python’s asyncio, and others have had to solve.

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain virtual memory and why every process gets its own address space
Describe how paging eliminates external fragmentation and how address translation works
Trace through a page fault and explain its performance impact using the EAT formula
Compare FIFO, OPT, and LRU page replacement algorithms and explain Belady’s Anomaly
Explain the causes of thrashing and the OS response
Calculate disk access times and compare FCFS, SCAN, C-SCAN, and SSTF scheduling

title: 08 · Memory Management
section: Your Program Is Living in a Lie
text:
Your Program Is Living in a Lie
When your C program accesses memory address 0x7fff5a2b3c40, it is not touching physical RAM at that address. In fact, two different processes running simultaneously might both use that exact address — and that’s fine, because neither is touching the same physical memory.
Your program operates inside a virtual address space: a fiction the OS maintains, mapping the addresses your program sees to wherever data actually lives in physical RAM (or on disk if swapped out). Every process gets its own complete virtual address space, starting at address 0. The mapping is managed transparently by OS and hardware — your program never has to think about it.
This illusion explains a lot: why programs can be larger than physical RAM, why one crashing process doesn’t corrupt another, why adding RAM makes the system faster, and why malloc can fail.






Opening Discussion



Before we explain virtual memory: on a 64-bit system, every process “sees” up to 2^64 bytes of address space. A 64-bit machine might have 16GB of physical RAM. How can dozens of processes each claim they have 2^64 bytes available? What has to be true about how they use that space for this to work?

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Requirements of Memory Management
Memory management must balance five competing demands simultaneously:
Relocation: a process doesn’t know in advance where it will be loaded. Different runs might land at entirely different physical addresses. All memory references must be translated correctly regardless.
Protection: a process must never access another process’s memory. The hardware checks every access — a significant ongoing cost for a critical safety property.
Sharing: processes should sometimes share memory — multiple instances of the same program can share code, and cooperative processes can share data. This requires controlled sharing without compromising protection elsewhere.
Logical organization: programs have structure (code, stack, heap, data). The memory model should reflect this rather than forcing everything into a flat uniform space.
Physical organization: programmers shouldn’t manage what’s in RAM vs. on disk. The OS handles this transparently.

title: 08 · Memory Management
section: Fixed and Dynamic Partitioning: Why They Failed
text:
Fixed and Dynamic Partitioning: Why They Failed
Early OSes divided physical memory into partitions — lessons from both approaches explain why virtual memory was necessary.
Fixed partitioning split RAM into static regions at boot. One process per partition. Problems: small processes in large partitions wasted space (internal fragmentation); large processes that didn’t fit couldn’t run; partition count limited multiprogramming.
Dynamic partitioning allocated exactly the memory each process needed. Eliminated internal fragmentation but created external fragmentation: as processes came and went at different sizes, memory filled with small unusable gaps. Compaction — moving processes to consolidate free space — was the fix, but it was expensive and disruptive.
Three placement algorithms emerged for dynamic partitioning: first-fit (use the first gap large enough), best-fit (use the smallest gap that fits, minimizing waste), next-fit (like first-fit but start from the last allocated point, spreading allocations throughout memory).

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Paging: The Solution That Stuck
Paging breaks both physical memory and the process’s virtual address space into fixed-size chunks of equal size — typically 4KB on modern systems. Physical chunks are frames; virtual chunks are pages.
The key insight: pages need not map to contiguous frames. Page 0 of your program might be in physical frame 47, page 1 in frame 2, page 3 in frame 891. The page table — maintained by the OS for each process — records this mapping. Address translation is done transparently by hardware (the Memory Management Unit, or MMU).
Address translation: a virtual address is split into a page number (high bits, index into the page table) and a page offset (low bits, byte position within the page). The page table maps page number → frame number. Physical address = frame_number × page_size + offset.






Board Exercise: Address Translation



Page size: 1KB (= 1024 bytes). Virtual address bits: 16 (so 6 bits page offset, 10 bits page number).
Given page table: page 0 → frame 3, page 1 → frame 7, page 2 → frame 1, page 3 → frame 5.
Translate these virtual addresses to physical: 1. Virtual address 1000 → page 0, offset 1000 → physical: 3×1024 + 1000 = 4072 2. Virtual address 1500 → page 1, offset 476 → physical: 7×1024 + 476 = 7644 3. Virtual address 3000 → page 2, offset 952 → physical: 1×1024 + 952 = 1976
(Paging eliminates external fragmentation entirely — why? Because any free frame can hold any page, regardless of size.)

title: 08 · Memory Management
section: Virtual Memory: Running Programs Larger Than RAM
text:
Virtual Memory: Running Programs Larger Than RAM
Paging enables something powerful: a page doesn’t need to be in physical RAM. It can live on disk, loaded only when the process actually accesses it. This is demand paging — the foundation of virtual memory.
Each page table entry has a valid/invalid bit: valid means the page is in RAM; invalid means it’s on disk or not yet allocated. When a process accesses an invalid page, the hardware generates a page fault. The OS handles it:

Trap to the OS, save registers and process state
Confirm it was a page fault; find the page’s location on disk
Find a free frame (evicting a page if necessary)
Initiate a disk read into that frame
Schedule another process while waiting for disk I/O
When the disk read completes, update the page table; resume the faulting process

The process never knows any of this happened. The memory access just took longer.
Effective Access Time (EAT): if p is the page fault rate, then:
EAT = (1 − p) × memory_access_time + p × page_fault_overhead
If memory access takes 100ns and a page fault takes 10ms, even a 0.1% fault rate increases average access time dramatically. Minimizing page fault rate is essential.
Copy-on-Write (COW): when fork() is called, the child and parent initially share the parent’s physical pages (marked read-only). Only when either process writes to a page does the OS create a private copy for the writer. Most fork/exec pairs never write to inherited pages — COW makes those forks nearly free.

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Page Replacement Algorithms
When a page fault occurs and no free frames exist, the OS must evict a page. The choice affects performance significantly.
FIFO: evict the oldest page. Simple. Suffers from Belady’s Anomaly — adding more frames can increase page faults for some reference patterns. This counterintuitive result disqualifies FIFO from serious use.
Optimal (OPT): evict the page not needed for the longest time in the future. Minimizes page faults provably. Impossible to implement (requires future knowledge). Used as a benchmark.
Least Recently Used (LRU): evict the page not accessed for the longest time. Uses the past as a proxy for the future — reasonable given locality of reference. Performs close to OPT in practice. Does not suffer Belady’s Anomaly. Implementation challenge: tracking recency without checking timestamps on every access.






Board Exercise: Page Replacement



Reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1
With 3 frames, calculate the number of page faults under: 1. FIFO 2. LRU 3. OPT
Compare the three. Notice that OPT serves as the theoretical minimum. How close does LRU get?
(Also try FIFO with 4 frames and note if Belady’s Anomaly appears — does adding a frame ever increase* page faults for this string?)*


Thrashing occurs when the OS spends more time swapping pages in and out than executing useful code. It happens when a process’s working set — the pages actively used in a time window — doesn’t fit in available frames. The process faults repeatedly; evicted pages are immediately needed again; CPU utilization collapses. The fix: reduce multiprogramming. Fewer active processes means each gets more frames, allowing working sets to fit in memory.

title: 08 · Memory Management
text:
Secondary Storage and Disk Scheduling
Virtual memory requires efficient disk access, so understanding disk performance is essential.
A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores data on spinning magnetic platters. Access time has three components:

Seek time — moving the arm to the right track (3–12ms typical)
Rotational latency — waiting for the sector to spin under the head (average = half a full rotation)
Transfer time — reading/writing the data once positioned (fast)

For a 7200 RPM disk: average rotational latency = ½ × (60s / 7200) = 4.17ms. Seek time dominates performance; minimizing unnecessary arm movement is the goal of disk scheduling.
FCFS: service requests in arrival order. Simple, but head movement can be large and erratic.
SCAN (elevator algorithm): sweep from one end to the other, servicing requests along the way, then reverse. Like an elevator — doesn’t skip back for requests behind it.
C-SCAN: like SCAN, but on the return trip the head jumps immediately back to the start without servicing. More uniform wait times — requests near one end don’t get double service.
SSTF (Shortest Service Time First): always service the nearest request to the current head position. Minimizes seek per request; can starve distant requests.






Board Exercise: Disk Scheduling



Request queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. Head starts at cylinder 53, moving upward.
For each algorithm, trace the head movement and compute total distance traveled: 1. FCFS 2. SCAN 3. C-SCAN 4. SSTF
Which minimizes total movement? Which gives the most uniform wait times? Which would you use on a heavy-write database server?
(Note: SSDs skip all of this analysis — no moving parts means seek time and rotational latency are essentially zero. Algorithms designed for HDDs are irrelevant to SSDs.)








Discussion Prompt



Chrome with 10 tabs open uses several gigabytes of RAM on a machine that has 16GB installed. Why? What’s actually in that memory? If you forced Chrome to run in only 1GB, what would happen at the OS level, and what would you observe from the user’s perspective?

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Explain what an OS does using the three-role framework (Referee, Illusionist, Glue)
Describe how multiprogramming improved CPU utilization over earlier batch systems
Place the memory hierarchy levels in order and explain the access/capacity tradeoff at each level
Define the process and virtual memory abstractions at a conceptual level

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
What Just Happened?
Double-click an app. The window appears. Simple.
Except it isn’t. In the fraction of a second between your click and that window, your operating system allocated memory, loaded executable code from disk, created a process, set up a virtual address space, wired up I/O channels, and handed off execution — all while continuing to run your music player, your browser, your clock, and everything else. None of that required any thought on your part.
This course is about understanding those thousand invisible things. Once you do, a lot of computing behavior that seemed arbitrary — why does your computer slow down with too many tabs open? why does your program crash with a segfault? why does adding more RAM help? — starts making sense.






Opening Discussion



Before moving forward: what do you think the OS is actually responsible for? What would break if it didn’t exist? Take a few guesses from the class before continuing.

title: 01 · OS Overview
section: What an Operating System Actually Is
text:
What an Operating System Actually Is
An operating system sits between hardware and the applications running on top of it. The hardware provides raw computational power. Applications want to use that power. The OS is the intermediary that makes the negotiation safe, efficient, and transparent.
It plays three distinct roles simultaneously:
Referee. Multiple programs run at the same time, and they all want the same resources: CPU time, memory, disk access, network bandwidth. Left to themselves, programs would constantly step on each other. The OS arbitrates access and enforces isolation — your text editor cannot read Chrome’s memory, and Chrome cannot starve your music player of CPU time.
Illusionist. Every running program believes it has exclusive access to the CPU and to a large, contiguous block of memory. Neither is true. The OS creates this illusion through scheduling and virtual memory, covered in depth in later lectures. Programmers can write code as if they own the machine, while the OS quietly ensures dozens of programs share it.
Glue. Hardware is diverse and messy. Your program shouldn’t need to know whether it’s writing to an NVMe SSD or a spinning hard drive, or whether its display is an OLED or an LCD. The OS provides a consistent set of abstractions — files, sockets, processes — that work regardless of what hardware is underneath.






Class Activity: Name That Role



For each of the following OS behaviors, identify which role it serves — Referee, Illusionist, or Glue. Discuss briefly:

Preventing Process A from reading Process B’s memory
Making printf() work on both Linux and macOS without code changes
Making a program think it has 8 GB of RAM on a machine with only 4 GB installed
Stopping a runaway process from using 100% of the CPU indefinitely

(These can overlap — some behaviors serve more than one role.)

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
OS Services
The OS provides services that applications depend on: an environment for program development and execution, I/O access, controlled access to the filesystem, system-wide access control, error detection, and resource accounting. These aren’t glamorous, but remove any one and software development gets dramatically harder. A single write() call, for instance, involves the OS arbitrating disk access, managing a buffer cache, handling errors, updating filesystem metadata, and ensuring other processes don’t clobber the same file simultaneously — all hidden behind a one-line API.

title: 01 · OS Overview
section: A Brief History of How We Got Here
text:
A Brief History of How We Got Here
Understanding the history makes the OS’s design decisions less arbitrary.
Serial Processing (1945–1955). No OS. Programmers reserved machine time on a sign-up sheet, walked in, set up their program physically, ran it, and collected output. Setup inefficiency and scheduling waste were enormous.
Simple Batch Systems (1955–1965). A monitor automated the transition between jobs. Programs were batched on tape and run sequentially without operator intervention. Better utilization, but the CPU still sat idle waiting for I/O.
Multiprogramming (1965–1980). The key insight: when one job waits for I/O, run a different job. Keep several programs in memory at once. Consider the numbers: if reading a file takes 15µs, executing 100 instructions takes 1µs, and writing takes 15µs, a single job keeps the CPU busy only about 3% of the time. With multiple jobs overlapping their I/O, CPU utilization climbs dramatically.
Time-Sharing (1970s–present). Multiprogramming maximized batch throughput, but interactive users needed fast response time. Time-sharing gave each user a short CPU slice in rapid rotation, creating the illusion of a dedicated machine. This is how your OS still works today.






Key Calculation: Multiprogramming Utilization



If a process spends fraction p of its time waiting for I/O, and there are n processes in memory, the probability all are waiting simultaneously is pn. CPU utilization ≈ 1 − pn.
Example on the board: 80% I/O wait (p = 0.8):

This is why adding more RAM (allowing more processes) directly improves CPU utilization — up to a point.

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
Processes and Memory: A Preview
Two abstractions appear throughout this course. A process is a running program — not just the code, but the program’s data, stack, heap, and all the OS bookkeeping: what it’s waiting for, what resources it holds, where it is in execution. Every program you launch becomes a process.
Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of its own large, private address space. The OS maps the addresses the program sees to wherever data actually lives in physical RAM or on disk. This is how programs whose combined memory needs exceed physical RAM can all run simultaneously.

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
The Memory Hierarchy
There is a fundamental and unavoidable tradeoff between speed and capacity that shapes every OS decision about memory:

The OS cannot change this hierarchy — it’s physics and economics. What it can do is manage movement between levels intelligently. The principle of locality makes this tractable: programs tend to access the same memory locations repeatedly in short time windows. Cache exploits this by keeping recently used data close to the CPU. Cache is entirely hardware-managed — the OS doesn’t control it — but understanding it is essential for writing efficient software and understanding system behavior.

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
Security, Fault Tolerance, and Scheduling
The OS handles security through the CIA triad: Confidentiality (only authorized users see data), Integrity (only authorized users modify data), and Availability (authorized users can access data reliably). It enforces all three through access control, process isolation, and virtual memory protection.
Fault tolerance keeps the system running when something breaks. Reliability R(t) is the probability of correct operation up to time t. Key metrics: Mean Time to Failure (MTTF) — how often things break — and Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) — how long to fix them. Availability = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR). Redundancy through backup components, data replication, and checkpointing is how high-availability systems achieve good numbers on these metrics.
Scheduling and resource management decide how CPU time, memory, and I/O are allocated. Fairness, efficiency, and responsiveness are all in tension — the right tradeoff depends entirely on the workload. Lectures 4 and 5 are dedicated to this.

title: 01 · OS Overview
text:
Multicore Considerations
Modern hardware has shifted dramatically toward many-core designs. Parallelism now exists at three levels: within a single instruction stream (handled by the CPU itself), across threads within a process, and across independent processes. The OS must assign work to many cores efficiently, synchronize shared data, and balance load — none of which is straightforward. This is one of the central engineering challenges in modern OS design.






Discussion Prompt



A student claims: “Since CPUs are so fast now, the overhead of scheduling and context switching is negligible.” How would you push back on that, using what you just learned about the memory hierarchy?

title: 02 · Processes
text:
Learning Objectives



By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

Describe the four memory regions that make up a process
Explain what information the PCB contains and why each field is necessary
Trace a process through its five lifecycle states and explain what triggers each transition
Walk through the steps of a context switch and explain why it has a performance cost
Explain what fork() does and the fork-exec pattern

title: 02 · Processes
text:
Open Your Task Manager
Press Ctrl+Shift+Esc on Windows, or run ps aux in a Linux terminal. What you see is a list of processes — every program the OS is currently tracking. There are probably 100–200 of them, even on a quiet system. For each one, the OS knows its ID, CPU usage, memory consumption, state, and dozens of other details.
The data structure that holds all of that information for a single process is called the Process Control Block (PCB), and it is the most important data structure in the OS. This lecture is about what’s in it, why, and how the OS uses it to manage dozens of running programs simultaneously.

title: 02 · Processes
text:
What a Process Is
A process is a program in execution. The distinction matters: a program is passive — an executable file sitting on disk. A process is active — that program loaded into memory, running or waiting to run, with its own dedicated state and resources.
Every process occupies four distinct regions in memory:

Text section — the executable instructions themselves
Data section — global variables and static data
Heap — dynamically allocated memory (malloc, new), grows and shrinks at runtime
Stack — local variables, function parameters, return addresses; a LIFO structure that grows with each function call and shrinks as they return

At any moment, the OS also tracks the process’s PID, current state, priority, program counter value, and the contents of all CPU registers. This execution context is what makes it possible to pause a process mid-execution, run something else, and resume later without the process knowing it was ever interrupted.






Quick Check



Draw a diagram of a process’s memory layout — text, data, heap, stack — and label which direction the heap and stack grow. Which two can collide if a program uses too much memory? This is a common interview question and a real system failure mode.

title: 02 · Processes
text:
The Process Control Block
The PCB is the OS’s per-process record. It’s a single data structure containing everything the OS needs to manage that process:
Process Identification — the numeric PID, the parent’s PID (PPID), and the user ID of the process owner.
Process State — one of five values: New, Ready, Running, Blocked/Waiting, or Terminated (described in the next section).
CPU Context — the values of all registers at the moment the process was last paused. When the process resumes, these get loaded back into the CPU. Without this, there would be no way to resume a process — the CPU state would be permanently lost.
Memory Information — where this process’s pages or segments live in physical memory, and the base/limit registers defining its valid address space.
Scheduling Information — the process’s priority, time spent waiting, time of last execution, and whatever other data the scheduling algorithm requires.
I/O Status — which files are open, which devices are in use, and any pending I/O requests.






The PCB’s Achilles Heel



Every running process is described by a PCB, and all PCBs are managed by the same kernel code. A bug in OS process management could corrupt every PCB simultaneously — crashing every process at once. This is why PCB-touching kernel code is among the most carefully written and tested code in existence. It is a genuine single point of failure for the entire system.

title: 02 · Processes
text:
Process States and Transitions
A process is always in exactly one of five states:

New — being created; the OS is allocating memory and initializing the PCB
Ready — in memory and ready to run, waiting for the scheduler
Running — instructions executing on a CPU core right now
Blocked (Waiting) — waiting for an external event (I/O, a signal, a lock); cannot proceed even if a CPU is available
Terminated — execution finished; OS is cleaning up







Board Exercise: Trace These Transitions



Work through the following scenario as a class and draw the state transitions:

The OS creates a new process for an app the user just launched
The scheduler selects it for execution
The process calls read() to load a file from disk
The disk I/O completes
The scheduler selects the process again
The process calls exit()

Which transition is most expensive? Which one is under the process’s control vs. the OS’s control?


Suspended processes add an extra layer. When memory is scarce, the OS can swap a blocked process out to disk entirely, freeing its RAM for others. The swapped process enters a Suspended state — not in memory, cannot run until swapped back in. Modern SSDs make this far less painful than it was in the spinning-disk era.

title: 02 · Processes
text:
The Context Switch
The context switch is how the CPU moves between processes. When the OS decides to switch from Process A to Process B:

Save A’s entire CPU state (all registers, program counter, flags) into A’s PCB
Update A’s state from Running to Ready or Blocked
Select Process B from the ready queue; update B’s state to Running
Load B’s CPU state from its PCB into the actual CPU registers
Jump to where B’s program counter points

From B’s perspective, it was never interrupted. The switch is invisible to both processes.
Context switches aren’t free. The save/restore takes time, and because B has different memory access patterns than A, much of the CPU cache is now stale — the first memory accesses will be slow cache misses. This is one reason modern OSes try to minimize unnecessary switches, and why thread switching (next lecture) is cheaper than full process switching.

title: 02 · Processes
02 · Processes
text:
Interrupts, Traps, and the Kernel
Three mechanisms let the CPU stop what it’s doing and handle something else:
Interrupts — asynchronous signals from hardware: a disk read completing, a timer firing, a network packet arriving. The CPU saves state and jumps to a kernel handler.
Traps — synchronous events from the current instruction: division by zero, segfault (invalid memory access), illegal instruction. The OS handles it, usually terminating the offending process.
System calls — explicit requests from a process to the kernel: open a file, allocate memory, fork a child. The process switches from user mode to kernel mode, the kernel does the work, and returns.
The kernel manages all of this — process creation and scheduling, memory management, I/O, and interrupt handling — running in privileged kernel mode with access to instructions user processes can never execute.






Live Demo



Run strace ls in a terminal (Linux/WSL). strace intercepts and prints every system call a process makes. You’ll see openat(), read(), write(), close(), and more — every interaction between ls and the kernel, completely exposed. Try it on other simple commands: strace echo hello, strace pwd. What’s the most surprising call you see?








Discussion Prompt



fork() creates a child with a copy of the parent’s address space. For a process using 2 GB of RAM, creating that copy sounds catastrophically slow. But fork() is actually fast. How? What optimization do modern OSes use to avoid eagerly copying all that memory? (This is worth working through carefully — the answer has implications for understanding both performance and the copy-on-write technique used throughout the kernel.)
